title: He Shipped Bed Warmers to the Tropics and Got Rich #history #shorts
description:
Timothy Dexter of Newburyport, Massachusetts, was a leather worker who could barely spell. He got rich on war money, and then, the story goes, on the worst business advice his rivals could think of. So was he a fool, or the luckiest man who ever lived?

Facts used: Dexter (1747-1806) bought up depreciated paper money after the Revolution. The federal government paid off the old Continental bills at about one cent on the dollar, but Massachusetts paid its own war notes in full. The coal-to-Newcastle story (his coal landing during a miners' strike) is a legend told in later accounts; it is not in his own book. In that book, A Pickle for the Knowing Ones (1802), Dexter wrote that he shipped about 42,000 warming pans to the West Indies, that people there used them for cooking, and that he cleared 79 percent (later tellers say they became molasses ladles). He bought a mansion on High Street, called himself Lord Timothy Dexter, and had about 40 wooden statues carved by the ship carver Joseph Wilson, among them Washington, Jefferson and Dexter himself, with a sign: "I am the first in the East, the first in the West, and the greatest philosopher in the Western world." The earliest accounts say he staged a mock funeral that about 3,000 people attended, then caned his wife for not crying. His book had no punctuation; a later edition added a page of punctuation marks for readers to "peper and solt it as they plese."

The scenes are an animated dramatization.
